Abstract 
Emotion identification acts as a critical component in passive brain-computer inter-
faces. The domain of EEG-based emotion identification has garnered substantial atten-
tion owing to advancements in machine learning models, notably in terms of higher 
accuracy and broader generalization capabilities. Current research investigates 
the utility of Tsallis entropy as an emotion recognition feature from EEG signals. For this 
study, different EEG rhythms are extracted via FIR filter and are normalized. Tsallis 
entropy is then computed using a sliding 4-s time window with a 2-s overlap, forming 
a feature vector for testing five machine learning models: K Nearest Neighbor (KNN), 
Support Vector Machine (SVM), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Naïve Bayes (NB), 
and Decision Trees (DT). Additionally, the ensemble models KNN-DT and DT-LDA are 
also analyzed. The SEED dataset is employed for this study, and performance is evalu-
ated through holdout cross-validation, considering accuracy, F1 score, precision, 
and recall metrices. Findings indicate that the DT-LDA ensemble model outperforms 
individual machine learning models and KNN-DT, achieving a significant accuracy 
increase of 5.6% to 11.2% for gamma rhythm. DT-LDA model displays the highest aver-
age classification accuracies 87.57% in gamma rhythm. This underscores the impor-
tance of high-frequency signals in emotion recognition, with gamma rhythm yielding 
the highest accuracy, while beta and all rhythms showing comparable results. These 
findings substantiate the efficacy of this methodology in the field of emotion identifi-
cation utilizing EEG signals.
Keywords:  Machine learning models, Emotion recognition, Tsallis entropy, 
Nonextensive statistics, Ensemble learning model
Introduction
As artificial intelligence has gained popularity, recognizing human emotions has become 
increasingly important in human–machine interactions [1]. Recognizing a person’s emo-
tional state can make the interaction more natural and user-friendly. The recognition 
of emotions involves the process of identifying and classifying emotions by considering 
data from physiology, behaviors and language [2]. This field has gained significance in 
recent years finding applications, in various areas such as healthcare, therapy, marketing 
and customer service industry [3, 4]. In healthcare industry by analysing physiological

and non-physiological emotion datasets, healthcare providers can identify patients who 
may be experiencing depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions [5–7]. This 
information can then personalize treatment plans and improve patient outcomes. Emo-
tion recognition is also used in the customer service industry, where companies use it to 
improve customer experiences [8–10]. By analysing customers’ emotions during inter-
actions, companies can understand customer needs and preferences and provide more 
personalized service.
Emotion recognition can be performed using physiological and non-physiological data 
[11–14]. Physiological data includes biometric signals that are generated by the body, 
such as heart rate [15], skin conductance [16], respiration [17], and body temperature. 
These signals provide information about a person’s internal physiological state and can 
be used to infer emotions such as stress, anxiety, and arousal. Non-physiological data, 
on the other hand, includes data that is generated by external behaviors, such as facial 
expressions [17, 18], body language [19, 20], speech pattern [21, 22], and text data [23]. 
These types of data provide information about a person’s external behaviors and can be 
used to infer emotions as well.
Utilizing physiological data for emotion recognition offers a notable advantage by fur-
nishing insights into an individual’s internal emotional state, which may not necessar-
ily be reflected in their observable behaviors. However, physical activity can also affect 
physiological data, making it challenging to infer emotions accurately [24]. This study 
concentrates on the application of EEG signals, extensively employed in emotion recog-
nition research. EEG, considered an intrusive method for assessing brain activity, holds 
promise for delivering real-time assessments of emotional states. The investigation of 
emotion recognition utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) signals has become a sig-
nificant area within affective computing research. EEG is gaining popularity in emotion 
recognition due to its simplicity, low cost, portability, ease of use, and, more importantly, 
reliability and accuracy [25]. In our current investigation, we utilize the SEED (SJTU 
Emotion EEG Dataset) for the study of emotion identification [26, 27].
Typically, when it comes to recognizing emotions based on EEG data there are two 
steps involved; extracting features and classifying emotions [28]. Feature extraction 
involves extracting meaningful information from raw EEG signals. This step is cru-
cial for effective emotion recognition because it determines the data quality used 
for classification. During feature extraction, researchers identify significant compo-
nents within EEG signals to facilitate emotion classification through feature vectors. 
These features could be divided in various subdomains like time-domain, frequency-
domain, and time–frequency domain characteristics [29]. For instance, prevalent 
time-domain features include Hjorth parameters, kurtosis, peak amplitude, wave 
duration, number of waves, mean, median, mode, and skewness [30, 31] while fre-
quency-domain features encompass power spectral density, phase coupling, reflection 
coefficients, and band power [32, 33]. Moreover, time–frequency domain features 
obtained through methodologies like the Hilbert Huang spectrum [34] are also 
employed. Recent investigations have underscored the complex nonlinear dynamics 
are inherent in EEG signals. Consequently, researchers are increasingly incorporat-
ing nonlinear features, such as hurst exponent, fractal spectrum, lyapunov exponents 
shannon entropy, C0-complexity, and differential entropy, recurrence rate to explore

Furthermore, researchers also tried to unfold the correlation among neurons incor-

non-extensive statistic has been introduced in biomedical signal processing, that out-
performs the existing EEG features for many EEG-based studies. In our investigation, 
Tsallis entropy is employed as a feature extracted from the EEG dataset to evaluate 
its efficacy in human emotion identification and assess its precision. A detailed math-
ematical explanation is given in "Data pre-processing" section.
After feature extraction, emotion classification is another crucial step. Numerous 
research studies are done on classification approaches. These approaches can be broadly 
categorized into three groups; machine learning models, deep learning models and 
ensemble learning models. Some of the widely used machine learning models, are Sup-
port Vector Machine (SVM) [37], K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) [38], Naive Bayes (NB) 
[39], Decision Tree (DT) [40], Perceptron [38], Logistic Regression [41]. Further came 
the development of deep learning classification methods, such as Feed forward neural 
network, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [42], recurrent neural network, deep 
belief networks(DBN) [43], graph CNNs [44], long short-term memory neural networks 
[45], autoencoders, and capsule networks [46]. Ensemble learning methods are the ones 
that use multiple learning algorithms to achieve better classification performance, such 
as bagging, boosting, and stacking models [47–50]. All these methods are being studied 
in the field of emotion recognition as well.
While deep learning methods are trending and being explored in emotion recognition, 
they often require significant computational resources and specialized knowledge to 
adjust hyperparameters effectively. As a result, traditional machine learning techniques 
are still frequently used for classification task. This research incorporates the utilization 
of five machine learning classifiers and then employs ensemble learning to amalgam-
ate the foremost three models (SVM, KNN, and NB) with the aim of enhancing per-
formance. The ensemble learning framework upholds commendable predictive accuracy 
and demonstrates robust generalization capabilities.
In the domain of emotion recognition classification, a key consideration lies in the 
categorization of classifiers as subject-dependent or subject-independent. A subject-
dependent approach involves training and testing the classifier using data from the same 
individual, while a subject-independent approach trains the classifier with data from 
multiple individuals and evaluates its performance on the data from different subjects 
who were not employed in the initial training process. The subject-dependent approach 
often yield better results since patterns in brain activity tend to be consistent within an 
individual making it easier to fit into statistical learning principles [51]. However, due to 
variations in EEG signals across individuals, subject independent classification becomes 
more challenging. While subject-dependent approaches may offer superior recognition 
accuracy, they often suffer from a lack of generalization, rendering them less suitable for 
real-world applications. In real world applications, emotional recognition systems often 
encounter circumstances wherein the training and testing datasets originate from dis-
tinct users. Consequently, the development of a subject-independent emotion recogni-
tion model has emerged as pivotal, garnering considerable attention among researchers. 
Hence, our study also adopts a subject-independent classification approach.

Methods
Stimuli, experiment and data acquisition
In this study, SEED dataset has been used. To collect this data, fifteen Chinese film 
excerpts representing a range of emotions—positive, neutral, and negative—were care-
fully selected to serve as stimuli for the experiments. Each clip, approximately 4 min 
in duration, was meticulously edited to ensure coherence in emotion elicitation and to 
maximize emotional significance. The experimental setup consisted of 15 trials, with 
each trial comprising a 5-s hint preceding the clip, followed by 45 s for self-assessment 
and a 15-s rest period after viewing as, shown in Fig. 2a. To prevent consecutive expo-
sure to clips targeting the same emotion, the order of presentation was thoughtfully 
arranged. Participants were instructed to complete a questionnaire immediately after 
each clip to report their emotional reactions. EEG data signals were recorded using a 
62-channel ESI NeuroScan System. The experimental setup and EEG electrode place-
ment are depicted in Fig. 2b. The study involved fifteen Chinese participants, consisting 
of 7 males and 8 females, with an average age of 23.27 years (standard deviation: 2.37).

Data pre‑processing
EEG datasets are high dimensional noisy neurophysiological signals. To prepare the data 
for analysis, artifacts, like eye movements (EOG) and muscle activity (EMG) and any 
interference from power lines are removed first. Then the data is downscaled to a sampling 
frequency of 200  Hz to simplify the feature extraction process. From each SEED trial, 
which lasts 4 min, a one-minute segment from the central part is extracted to maintain 
data uniformity. Using a FIR filter, EEG rhythms such as theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–15 Hz), 
beta (16–31  Hz), gamma (32–75  Hz) are extracted from preprocessing signal. Prior to 
feature extraction from EEG rhythms, the data undergoes normalization utilizing the 
z-score method, expressed as follows for a random variable ’Y’ with mean ’Ῡ’ and standard

This normalization technique helps remove subject bias and allows more meaningful 
comparisons between different individuals while maintaining channel variability. Subse-

Tsallis entropy is non-extensive and adheres to the pseudo-additivity rule [53]:
In the above equation, q serves as a parameter quantifying the degree of non-extensiv-
ity [56]. When q = 1, it denotes extensivity. Conversely, for, q < 1 it signifies super-exten-
sivity, while for q > 1 it indicates sub-extensivity.
Tsallis’s work generalizes Boltzmann–Gibbs statistics, aptly explaining systems with 
long-range interactions [53]. Though this generalization has been known in the thermo-
dynamic context from former centuries, it is now gaining broader applicability. Tsallis 
Entropy has recently been extensively adopted in biomedical fields like ECG [57] and 
EEG [58, 59] signal processing. Research findings have shown that Tsallis entropy can 
yield the system’s enhanced technicalities than the traditional Shannon entropy [57, 58, 
60]. EEG data, reflecting large-scale interactions among billions of neurons, inherently 
exhibits long-range correlations, necessitating a non-extensive approach [61]. Moreover, 
since there is mutual information between the various neural populations, it is fair to 
classify EEG as a sub-extensive framework (i.e. q > 1) [58, 59].
It can be inferenced, Tsallis entropy is helpful in studying the brain due to its ability to 
capture the complexity, non-extensive behaviour, and long-range dependencies of brain 
signals. It enables researchers to analyze brain activity in a more comprehensive and 
nuanced manner, detect abnormalities, explore brain connectivity, and investigate cog-
nitive states and information processing. In this study, the objective is to derive a tempo-
ral evolution of Tsallis entropy by integrating a sliding time window into the input signal, 
followed by averaging the entropy values obtained from the buffered signal. This average 
Tsallis entropy acts as an indicator of abnormalities in the EEG signal under analysis and 
assists in distinguishing between the two emotions, across different EEG rhythms.
Classification models
Once the relevant features have been extracted, they can be used to train a classifier to 
recognize emotional states. The accuracy of an emotion recognition system can be sig-
nificantly influenced by the quality of extracted features and the selection of classifiers. 
In our study, we assess five commonly utilized conventional classifiers: KNN, SVM, NB, 
LDA, and DT with Tsallis entropy feature.

KNN classifier
The K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier stands as a fundamental machine learning 
algorithm utilized in both classification and regression tasks [63, 65]. In classification, 
KNN assigns a class label to a given data point by assessing the majority class among 
its K nearest neighbors within the feature space. The algorithm retains all available data 
points along with their associated class labels. When presented with a new data point, 
the algorithm computes distances between this point and every other point in the train-
ing set, employing metrics such as Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, or cosine 
similarity and others. KNN selects the K nearest data points based on these calculated 
distances. Unlike certain other algorithms, KNN does not entail explicit model training, 
thereby facilitating rapid adaptation to new data. The choice of K value in KNN is piv-
otal; a smaller K value increases susceptibility to noise, while a larger value elevates com-
putational complexity and may lead to excessive smoothing. In this study, computational 
optimization for the considered data led us to select ’k = 10’ as the number of neighbors 
and ’Euclidean’ as the distance metric. defined as Distance

Decision trees classifier
A decision tree is a tree-like structure that uses a series of decision rules to predict the 
target variable by recursively splitting the data into smaller subsets based on the most 
significant features/attributes [66, 67]. Decision Trees work by initializing the root node 
with the entire data set. It then selects the best feature/attribute to split the data based 
on the highest information gain or reduction in impurity (e.g., Gini index, entropy). Fur-
ther, the data is partitioned into subsets based on the selected feature’s values, and each 
subset is assigned to a child node. The process is repeated for each child node until a 
stopping criterion is met (e.g., minimum number of samples in a leaf node, maximum 
tree depth). At each leaf node, the target variable based on the majority class is assigned 
its class. Pictorial representation of DT classifier is shown in Fig. 3.
Linear discriminant analysis
Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) serves as a supervised machine learning algo-
rithm tailored for classification tasks [33, 50]. Its primary objective is to ascertain a 
linear combination of features that maximally discriminates between two or more 
classes of objects or events. Within LDA, the aim is to identify a data projection that 
maximizes the separation between the means of distinct classes while minimizing 
intra-class variance. This projection facilitates the classification of new data points 
based on their position relative to the decision boundary. LDA operates under the 
assumption of normal data distribution and equal covariance matrices across classes. 
It computes the mean and covariance matrix for each class, subsequently deriving a 
linear discriminant function to map the data onto a new coordinate system. During 
training, the LDA algorithm learns optimal coefficients for this discriminant function. 
Upon encountering new data, LDA applies this function and compares the resulting 
value to a decision threshold for classification. LDA is valued for its simplicity and

Ensemble learning
Ensemble machine learning combines multiple models to solve a classification prob-
lem [51, 68]. Ensemble learning improves the model’s accuracy by combining different 
models trained on the same data set but using different algorithms or variations of the 
same algorithm. The idea behind ensemble learning is that when different models are 
combined, their strengths are amplified, and their weaknesses are reduced. Ensemble 
classifiers can be divided into two categories: bagging and boosting. Bagging: In this 
technique, multiple models are trained on different subsets of the training data, and 
their results are combined to get the final prediction. Bagging can be used with any 
classification algorithm, and it effectively reduces the model’s variance, which means 
it makes the model more stable and less prone to overfitting. Boosting: Boosting is a 
type of self-learning method that utilizes weighted assignments for different elements 
in the dataset. Initially, all items are given equal weights, but as each model is gener-
ated, a weight is assigned based on performance.
Additionally, misclassified data are given more weight after each model evalua-
tion, which allows the next model to concentrate more on these misclassified data. In 
each iteration, the technique calculates weights for each training example based on 
the degree of its misclassification, constructs a hypothesis, and adjusts the hypoth-
esis’s weight accordingly. Ultimately, the final model is created by combining differ-
ent models focusing on other data groups through voting based on their weights. The 
final model is averaged by using the weighted average method.

Metrics for performance evaluation
Performance evaluation metrics measure the accuracy, effectiveness, and efficiency 
of a machine learning model. These metrics are important to evaluate the quality of 
a classifier’s predictions and to compare different classifiers or models. These metrics 
include:

Accuracy: Accuracy, a metric widely utilized in classification tasks, quantifies the pro-
portion of correctly classified instances. It holds relevance for balanced datasets, being a 
prevalent measure of performance. Nonetheless, accuracy may prove misleading when 
confronted with imbalanced datasets.
Precision: Precision quantifies the ratio of true positives to the total number of pre-
dicted positives. This metric proves valuable in contexts where the expense associated 
with false positives is significant.
Sensitivity: Sensitivity quantifies the ratio of true positives to the total actual posi-
tives. This metric proves valuable in situations where the ramifications of false negatives 
carry significant consequences.
F1-score: The F1-score represents the harmonic mean of precision and recall, serving 
as a valuable metric in situations where both precision and recall hold significance.
These metrics should be selected based on the problem’s context and the project’s spe-
cific needs. Choosing the right metrics to evaluate the classifier’s performance correctly 
is essential.
Results and discussions
The SEED dataset comprises EEG signals of three emotional states: positive, neutral, and 
negative. The present study considers only the positive and negative samples, resulting 
in a total of (15*10*3) 450 samples of datasets. Using the FIR filter, every trial from all 15 
subjects was decomposed into four frequency bands: theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–15 Hz), 
beta (16–31 Hz), and gamma (32–75 Hz). The SEED dataset comprises EEG data from 
62 channels, giving 62 feature vectors for a single trial. A total of 27,900 feature vec-
tors were computed from each rhythm for the two emotion states. Furthermore, concat-
enated feature vectors from all four rhythms were combined to form a 1,11,600-feature 
vector for all trials. The study is performed in two experiments: one is comparing accu-
racy from four EEG rhythms, and the other is comparing accuracy, F1 score, Precision 
and recall in individual best performing gamma rhythms.

3% to 10% for the theta rhythm, 3% to 7% for the alpha rhythm, 2.4% to 9.2% for the beta 
rhythm, and 5.6% to 11.2% for the gamma rhythm. The highest and average classifica-
tion accuracies achieved by the DT-LDA model for theta, alpha, beta, gamma, and all 
rhythms are 60.24%, 65.38%, 80.57%, 87.59%, and 84.91%, respectively.
Illustrations in Fig. 4a–e collectively suggest that the DT-LDA ensemble model yields 
the most favourable classification outcomes for each distinct rhythm. In emotion rec-
ognition, using higher-frequency rhythm data delivers optimal classification results. A 
comparative analysis against prior studies in Table 3 demonstrates that our proposed 
DT-LDA ensemble learning model, which incorporates Tsallis entropy features, achieves 
heightened accuracy and stability when applied to SEED datasets. Considering the pre-
sented experimental outcomes, it is evident that our method is exceptionally well-suited 
for subject-independent emotion classification tasks shows in Fig. 5.

across domains like mental health, human–computer interaction, and entertainment. In 
our investigation, we assess the effectiveness of Tsallis entropy as a feature in conjunc-
tion with five fundamental conventional machine learning classifiers (SVM, DT, LDA, 
KNN, NB). Additionally, we combine the three most suitable classifiers into an ensem-
ble classifier (DT-LDA, KNN-LDA) for EEG-based emotion recognition. Our methodol-
ogy involves extracting Tsallis entropy features from pre-processed data and employing 
a sliding time window to capture the temporal characteristics of EEG signals better. The 
SEED dataset serves as the testing ground for our experiments.
Notably, the results illustrate that Tsallis entropy, in conjunction with the DT-LDA 
ensemble learning model, outperforms individual models in terms of accuracy, preci-
sion, recall and Fscore. The experimental findings are encouraging, culminating with the 
highest classification accuracy reaching 87.59%. Notably, low-frequency rhythms convey 
considerably less information than their high-frequency and all frequency counterparts. 
However, a comparison between the findings of this study and those of prior research, as 
outlined in Table 3, reveals that Tsallis entropy offers performance that competes effec-
tively with a range of contemporary techniques. Particularly noteworthy is its aptitude 
for cross subject emotion classification tasks, as evidenced by the outcomes demon-
strated. This investigation suggests promising avenues for the development of resilient 
and precise emotion recognition systems, thus facilitating a multitude of practical 
applications.

Abstract: Emotion identification acts as a critical component in passive brain-computer inter- faces. The domain of EEG-based emotion identification has garnered substantial atten- tion owing to advancements in machine learning models, notably in terms of higher accuracy and broader generalization capabilities. Current research investigates the utility of Tsallis entropy as an emotion recognition feature from EEG signals. For this study, different EEG rhythms are extracted via FIR filter and are normalized. Tsallis entropy is then computed using a sliding 4-s time window with a 2-s overlap, forming a feature vector for testing five machine learning models: K Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Decision Trees (DT). Additionally, the ensemble models KNN-DT and DT-LDA are also analyzed. The SEED dataset is employed for this study, and performance is evalu- ated through holdout cross-validation, considering accuracy, F1 score, precision, and recall metrices. Findings indicate that the DT-LDA ensemble model outperforms individual machine learning models and KNN-DT, achieving a significant accuracy increase of 5.6% to 11.2% for gamma rhythm. DT-LDA model displays the highest aver- age classification accuracies 87.57% in gamma rhythm. This underscores the impor- tance of high-frequency signals in emotion recognition, with gamma rhythm yielding the highest accuracy, while beta and all rhythms showing comparable results. These findings substantiate the efficacy of this methodology in the field of emotion identifi- cation utilizing EEG signals.
